stories.author: ComputedCamp995
stories.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
stories.groq_label: DeepCrossAttention replaces static residual adds with dynamic cross‑layer attention, delivering similar or better model quality up to three times faster while cutting parameters by 30‑40%.
stories.groq_explain:
Google’s research blog entry describes a new architecture called DeepCrossAttention (DCA) that improves the way transformer models use residual, or “skip,” connections. The article begins by explaining that traditional deep learning models suffer from vanishing gradients because information degrades as it passes through many layers. Transformers mitigate this by adding the input of a layer to its output via a simple point‑wise sum, but this uniform weighting can dilute important high‑resolution details from earlier layers.

The authors’ ICML 2025 paper identifies this limitation and proposes DCA, which replaces the fixed additive residual with a dynamic routing mechanism that selects and combines features from the entire history of preceding layers on a per‑token basis. DCA introduces two key components. First, dynamic layer routing computes token‑specific mixing weights using a static learnable base plus an input‑dependent projection, allowing the network to adapt its processing structure from sequential to parallel as needed. Second, depth‑wise cross‑attention applies an attention operation across layers rather than across tokens, letting each token query a weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings without the heavy computational cost of conventional attention.

Experiments on synthetic tasks, large‑scale language modeling benchmarks (C4 and LM1B), and image classification demonstrate that DCA speeds up convergence, improves training stability, and yields higher final model quality. On the LM1B benchmark, DCA reaches the same perplexity as a standard transformer in roughly one‑fifth the number of training steps, and it achieves a lower perplexity with 30 layers compared with 42 layers required by a baseline transformer, reducing depth and parameter count by about 29 %. The method adds less than 0.2 % extra parameters, so its impact on compute and memory is negligible while increasing memory bandwidth because representations from different layers remain intact.

Because DCA can be initialized to behave exactly like a standard residual network, it can be retrofitted onto pre‑trained transformers and fine‑tuned, delivering a perplexity reduction of 0.19 on LM1B versus only 0.02 from continued standard training. The article argues that dynamic residual routing such as DCA is becoming an important trend for scaling large language models, noting that related work from Moonshot AI—attention residuals—shares the principle of replacing blind addition with selective attention‑based retrieval, further preventing hidden‑state growth and information dilution. Overall, the post highlights DCA as a lightweight yet powerful enhancement that offers comparable or better model quality while accelerating training by up to three times.

stories.author: mmcclure
stories.title: Tabernetes: A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
stories.groq_label: Tabernetes lets browser tabs act as Kubernetes nodes by booting a Linux kernel in WebAssembly to run pods.
stories.groq_explain:
Tabernetes is a project that turns individual web browser tabs into nodes of a Kubernetes cluster. When a user opens the page, the browser tab can register itself as a node, and the Kubernetes scheduler can assign a pod to that tab. The pod’s program runs inside a Linux kernel that is compiled to WebAssembly and boots inside the tab, using the tab’s CPU and memory. When the tab is closed, the node disappears and the scheduler relocates the pod to another available tab. 

To join the cluster, a user scans a QR code or uses the same browser they are reading the page with. The joining process downloads about five megabytes and starts a small Linux guest that runs on a single core until the tab is closed. The control plane remains a standard Kubernetes installation, while a custom container runtime called tabc launches containers inside the browser tabs. Pods are defined like any other Kubernetes pod, with the addition of a runtimeClassName set to “tab” to indicate that they should run in a browser tab.

The interface shows statistics such as the number of nodes, pods, and countries participating, as well as metrics for boot time, pod movement, and overall cluster age, all of which are currently at zero because no tabs have joined yet. The topology diagram visualizes the control plane in the center, with each tab represented as a node and services connecting to pods behind those nodes. An orange dot indicates a request traveling to a pod, while a green dot shows a picture tile being sent to a rendering node.

Overall, Tabernetes demonstrates a novel way to leverage the ubiquitous presence of web browsers to provide distributed compute resources for Kubernetes workloads, turning everyday browsing sessions into a volunteer compute grid. It highlights the feasibility of running Linux kernels in WebAssembly within browsers and integrates this capability into existing Kubernetes scheduling and management mechanisms.

stories.author: rbanffy
stories.title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
stories.groq_label: 9/UX implements a Macintosh style spatial desktop on 9front using a rio fork, libux and 9P based UI integration
stories.groq_explain: The page introduces 9/UX, a Macintosh‑inspired desktop environment created for the 9front operating system. It runs a fork of the rio window system in a special 9/UX mode, adding a global menu bar, title‑bar chrome, a drag broker and a spatial desktop with volume icons, folder windows, rename, duplicate, Get Info, Trash and remembered layout. The interface follows the classic Mac and A/UX style—global menus, consistent controls and dialogs, icons and resource‑driven presentation—while preserving native 9front programs and existing rio applications unchanged. All user‑interface elements are exposed as Plan 9 files: 9P presents each application’s UI state and commands, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb stores human‑editable metadata. The system includes a libux toolbox that provides windows, menus, dialogs, alerts and controls, each app serving its control tree over 9P so that actions such as pressing a button can be performed by writing to a control file. The uxd daemon aggregates the trees, uxmeta tracks associations, volumes and layout, resfs serves classic icon and string resources, and clipd implements a typed clipboard synchronized with rio’s snarf. A live demonstration runs entirely in the browser using h9, a 386 emulator that loads a compiled 386 binary of the rio fork and a sample libux application. The demo requires a recent Chrome or Edge browser and loads about 23 MB once; it shows real interaction with mouse clicks, keyboard input and 9P file operations, and a screenshot is shown for other browsers. Screenshots and visual design details illustrate that the graphics use a sixteen‑colour palette, whole‑pixel drawing and original icons, matching classic Macintosh metrics but without Apple resources. Documentation includes a design document outlining acceptance criteria, release notes, protocol specifications and visual design guidelines. Source code is hosted on GitHub under an MIT license, with development scripts that clone and build the h9 emulator and the rio binaries directly from the host shell. The project is marked as version 0.1 and under active development, with a warning that interfaces may change and users are encouraged to report bugs via GitHub issues. Credits note the pixel‑art menu‑bar mark created by Dan Fessler and the Plan 9 bunny Glenda by Renée French. Related links point to h9, native 9front executables and the historical A/UX system.

stories.author: DeepLogin
stories.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
stories.groq_label: Virginia and Oregon attorneys general sued SpaceX for allowing Grok to produce and share child sexual abuse material and non‑consensual sexual images.
stories.groq_explain:
The page is a press release from the Commonwealth of Virginia Office of the Attorney General announcing that Attorney General Jay Jones, together with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, has filed a civil lawsuit against SpaceX, the company that now operates the social network X, its artificial‑intelligence division xAI (renamed “SpaceX Super Intelligence”) and the Grok family of large‑language models.  

The complaint alleges that SpaceX and its subsidiaries knowingly failed to protect users by allowing Grok to generate sexualized images, including child sexual‑abuse material (CSAM) and non‑consensual intimate imagery (NCII), while publicly claiming that robust safeguards were in place. The suit says the company promoted a “spicy mode” that encouraged the creation of nude or sexual content and marketed Grok as a rebellious AI companion, fully aware that the technology could be used to produce illegal and harmful images.  

A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm is cited, estimating that between December 29, 2025 and January 8, 2026 Grok produced roughly three million sexualized images on X, about 23 000 of which appeared to depict children. That equates to about 190 sexualized images per minute and one child‑related image every 41 seconds. Nearly a third of the child images identified remained publicly accessible a week after detection, and many “removed” images could still be reached via alternate URLs.  

The attorneys general argue that SpaceX’s lack of industry‑standard safeguards was intentional, describing it as a “feature, not a bug,” and that the company deceived consumers about safety while exposing millions of users in Virginia, Oregon and elsewhere to harmful content and the risk that their own photos could be manipulated without consent.  

The Virginia suit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond, and the Oregon suit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court. The filing is presented as the first step toward holding the company accountable for alleged violations of consumer‑protection and child‑exploitation laws.  

The release underscores the broader significance of regulating powerful AI tools, emphasizing the need for legal accountability when tech firms prioritize growth over user safety and fail to prevent the creation and distribution of illegal sexual content.

stories.author: ok123456
stories.title: The AT&T Unix PC (3B1) VM
stories.groq_label: A FreeBee fork enhances the AT&T UNIX PC (3B1) emulator with Ethernet, TCP/IP, seamless mouse handling, and significant speed improvements
stories.groq_explain:
The article is a guest post by Tenox describing a new, highly enhanced virtual machine for the AT&T UNIX PC, also known as the PC 7300 or 3B1, a 1985 Unix desktop originally developed by Convergent Technologies and sold by AT&T. Emulating the 3B1 has been possible for years, with early efforts such as Phil Pemberton’s FreeBee project beginning in 2010 and subsequent milestones achieved by various contributors who got the diagnostic disk, AT&T UNIX, and a C compiler running. However, previous versions lacked networking and required cumbersome mouse handling.

Tenox’s fork of FreeBee adds Ethernet support and a full TCP/IP stack using a virtual 3B1 Ethernet board derived from MAME and libslirp. With this, the classic WIN/TCP suite can perform telnet, FTP and remote shell connections to the Internet. The mouse now works seamlessly without the old F10 grab, and the scroll wheel functions. Performance has been dramatically improved: the virtual CPU can run up to thirty‑two times faster than the original hardware while keeping the clock in real time, and an idle VM consumes only about four percent of a Mac core compared with the forty‑four percent required by earlier emulations.

Additional fixes eliminate frozen Office forms, stuck Alt keys and screen flicker on macOS. The fork also provides scripting capabilities through a control socket and an MCP server, and includes a pull request that contributes the changes back to the upstream FreeBee project.

The distribution ships a complete UNIX System V 3.51m image with Fix Disk 2.0 and 187 software packages, covering almost every program that ever ran on the UNIX PC. Included are Microsoft Word, Multiplan, dBASE III, WordStar 2000, GCC 2.5.8, GNU Emacs 19, TeX, and more than eighty games. The image is assembled from the 3B1 archive, Arnold Robbins’ and Alain Knaff’s disk collections, and the VCF.

The author showcases the system running in resizable windows, with the classic 720×348 one‑bit screen, a 10 MHz 68010 CPU (emulated ten times faster), 4 MB of RAM, a 195 MB virtual disk, and the new Ethernet board. System panels, Office preferences, and Ethernet configuration windows can be moved and overlapped with the mouse. Demonstration programs include graphical effects such as a 3‑D cosine plot, spirograph output, and a multitasking demo.

Productivity applications appear in full‑screen mode: Microsoft Word 1.10, Microsoft Multiplan 1.20, and the AT&T Memohead form editor. Tenox also adds new native 3B1 games created in 2026, including 2048, Bubble Breaker, Falling Blocks, Snake and Sokoban, each with multiple levels and AI‑generated content.

Because the original WIN/TCP telnet client cannot handle modern servers, Tenox wrote a replacement called telnetu, which offers a VT100/xterm terminal, UTF‑8 support, DNS resolution, and both fullscreen and windowed modes. It can be used to access services such as mapscii.me, Alpine Linux’s htop, and the telehack.com aquarium.

A tiny web browser named Archaic has been built for the 3B1’s WRP environment. It renders web pages on the host machine, then sends a picture of the rendered page back to the 3B1 with clickable links, allowing the legacy system to browse modern sites like its own Wikipedia entry.

For fun, Tenox patched the kernel, window driver and shared library to support a “tall screen” mode of 720 × 696 pixels, effectively doubling the vertical resolution. This experimental build is provided as a separate branch and image.

Ready‑to‑run portable images are available for macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux (x64 and arm64) and Windows (x64). After unpacking, the user runs a simple script, logs in as “tenox” for the Office environment or “root” for a shell, and no passwords are required. The article supplies direct download links for the standard image, the tall‑screen hack, and the source repository of the FreeBee fork.

Overall, the post highlights how a combination of community contributions, modern emulation techniques and new networking support have turned the AT&T UNIX PC into a fully functional, fast, and feature‑rich virtual machine that can run historic software and even new applications created for the platform. This matters because it preserves a unique piece of computing history while making it accessible on contemporary hardware.

stories.author: MickyTheMouse
stories.title: Convex skills send the user's app idea to a remote server without telling them
stories.groq_label: Convex plugin skills covertly transmit user project ideas to an external server and run unverified remote scripts, creating privacy and security risks.
stories.groq_explain: The issue report describes a privacy and security concern in three Convex backend skills that are published in Anthropic’s Claude‑plugins marketplace. In the quick‑start skill, the user’s one‑sentence project idea is sent via an HTTP POST request to a remote server at basic‑anteater‑667.convex.site, which is labeled in the code as telemetry. The user is not informed that this data leaves their machine. Two other skills download a script from the same host and pipe it directly into a Bash shell, and a third skill splits the download and execution into separate Bash calls, explicitly advising developers to avoid a single command that both fetches and runs code because such a pattern would be blocked by safety classifiers. This instruction effectively circumvents the user’s safety tooling, allowing unpinned code from a dynamically generated host to run without any opportunity for the user or an administrator to review it. The report includes excerpts of the relevant shell code that demonstrate how the idea is posted, how the bootstrap script is fetched and executed, and how the “shape harness safety classifiers” are deliberately avoided. The author recommends notifying the user before transmitting their idea, making the telemetry optional, bundling or hash‑pinning the bootstrap scripts within the plugin, and removing the classifier‑bypass instruction so that the download‑and‑run step can be subject to normal safety checks. The issue matters because it exposes users to unintended data collection and potentially unsafe code execution, undermining trust in the plugin ecosystem and bypassing security mechanisms that users may rely on. The report also notes that the problematic code remains on the main branch as of late October and that the author maintains a catalog of agent skills where this finding is listed.

stories.author: scanr
stories.title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
stories.groq_label: Credit card skimming scripts leveraging WebRTC were discovered on several major retail sites and removed prior to Black Friday.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that a malicious credit‑card‑skimming script exploiting WebRTC was discovered on the checkout pages of several well‑known online retailers in the week leading up to Black Friday. The script was found on Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD. After InfoHawk alerted the affected companies, all of the scripts were removed on November 24th or 25th, before the holiday shopping rush.

The skimmer was designed to capture a shopper’s card number, expiration date, security code, as well as personal information such as name, address, phone and email. It transmitted these details to a third‑party server the moment the user entered them, before the store’s payment gateway could validate the transaction. This means a card could be stolen even if the order was later declined or cancelled, leaving the shopper unaware of any problem.

The attack vector relied on WebRTC, the browser technology normally used for video calls. By opening a WebRTC data channel, the malicious code could bypass typical content‑security‑policy rules that monitor ordinary web requests. The loader reached the checkout pages through various means, including consent‑banner settings, retailer CDN files, shared marketing pixels or the site’s own HTML. Once loaded, the script fetched additional code from Amazon S3 buckets, then established a WebRTC connection via Cloudflare’s TURN relay. The code was delivered in encrypted chunks, verified with a SHA‑256 hash, and executed with eval. Card details were sent back over the same WebRTC channel. The only live capture observed was on Lascana’s checkout page, where test card data was transmitted to the attacker.

The report lists the status of each compromised site at the time of publication: Lascana and the Quorum marketing pixel were altered and removed on November 24; Samsonite and American Tourister’s cookie‑consent settings were edited and the code was removed on the same day; Revolve and FWRD had altered files on their own CDNs and confirmed removal on November 25. InfoHawk also notified Amazon Web Services, Cloudflare, domain registrars, the pixel vendor and the consent‑banner provider.

For consumers, the article advises checking recent statements for unauthorized charges, contacting the bank or card issuer promptly, and filing a dispute within 60 days. It notes that U.S. federal law limits liability for unauthorized credit‑card charges to $50, often zero for card‑number‑only theft, while debit‑card protections are weaker and depend on timely reporting.

Finally, the piece urges site owners to immediately audit and remove any unauthorized scripts, tighten content‑security‑policy rules, monitor WebRTC traffic, and work with hosting and CDN providers to prevent similar attacks in the future.

stories.author: tylermw
stories.title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
stories.groq_label: Rayshader 1.0 brings cinematic 3D ray‑traced mapping to R, simplifying data visualization and powering high‑profile news graphics.
stories.groq_explain:
The post introduces the 1.0 release of the R package rayshader, describing it as a major step toward eliminating the “Matrix problem” that has long made the tool difficult to use. The author recounts how rayshader began eight years ago as a small experiment that combined ray‑tracing with cartographic hill‑shading, turning ordinary elevation matrices into striking 3‑D visualizations directly inside R. Early versions required users simply to feed a numeric matrix, add layers, and call plot_3d() to produce a 3‑D landscape, and that simplicity attracted many hobbyists and social‑media creators.

The narrative then shifts to how journalists quickly adopted the package because its visual appeal could capture attention. Notable examples include a Wall Street Journal feature on Arctic shipping, a Bloomberg story visualizing the rubble in Gaza, and a front‑page flood map for The Sydney Morning Herald. These uses demonstrated that rayshader could move from “fun posts” to serious public‑interest reporting, but they also exposed significant workflow friction. In deadline‑driven newsrooms, any extra step—such as manually converting coordinate systems, cropping data, or tweaking render parameters—can be prohibitive.

The core source of that friction, according to the author, is rayshader’s reliance on plain matrices to represent terrain. Real‑world spatial data typically arrives as georeferenced rasters, vectors, or point clouds with assorted coordinate reference systems and units (meters, feet, degrees, even German legal metres). Users must repeatedly convert these inputs into matrices, remember extents, manage CRS information, adjust scales, and correct orientation errors, a process that is both error‑prone and time‑consuming. The author describes this as a usability red flag that hampers both beginners and experienced users.

Version 1.0 is presented as a redesign that removes much of that overhead. Although the article cuts off before detailing the specific changes, it promises a new API that handles spatial bookkeeping internally, letting users concentrate on presentation rather than data wrangling. The release is positioned as an effort to make high‑quality, ray‑traced visualizations accessible to a broader audience, especially those who need fast, reliable output for journalism and other time‑sensitive applications.

The page ends abruptly, so the exact list of new features and technical implementations is not provided. However, the overall message is clear: the 1.0 update aims to streamline the workflow, reduce the reliance on manual matrix conversion, and solidify rayshader’s role as a practical tool for creating beautiful, data‑driven 3‑D visualizations directly within R.

stories.author: robtherobber
stories.title: Paolo Soleri built a utopian eco-city in the Arizona desert
stories.groq_label: Arcosanti is Paolo Soleri's experimental Arizona eco city built on arcology principles that was planned for five thousand residents but peaked at about one hundred fifty
stories.groq_explain:
Paolo Soleri, an Italian architect who studied under Frank Lloyd Wright, began constructing Arcosanti in 1970 as a prototype eco‑city in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona. Inspired by his concept of “arcology” – a fusion of architecture and ecology outlined in his 1969 book – Soleri envisioned a dense, three‑dimensional community for 5,000 residents that would counter the spread of suburban sprawl. The unfinished 860‑acre site consists of earth‑cast concrete apses, vaulted arches and Brutalist forms that rise amid cypress trees, with public, semi‑public and private spaces arranged vertically. 

In practice the settlement never attracted more than about 150 people and today only a few dozen “Arconauts” live there, sharing communal facilities such as a library, gym, farmers’ market and weekly gatherings. Residents like Manny Garcia, a millennial who works in the on‑site foundry, and artist Yvonne Brook, who lives in a two‑bedroom unit allocated by a seniority committee, describe the lifestyle as simple, creative and cooperative, offering an antidote to the high cost of housing and growing isolation in contemporary society. The article links Arcosanti’s principles to today’s housing crisis, noting that soaring home prices and post‑pandemic loneliness have spurred interest in co‑living, intentional communities and high‑end shared‑amenity developments such as London’s Ark tower. 

The piece also highlights Soleri’s critique of urban expansion, quoting his belief that spreading out “kills culture,” and underscores the relevance of his ideas as cities continue to grow while environmental concerns mount. An upcoming exhibition in London, “An Earthly Paradise,” will explore similar experiments in housing and social organization, reinforcing the broader cultural shift toward fluid living arrangements, shared resources and communal resilience. Arcosanti remains a living laboratory for density, sustainability and shared humanity, illustrating both the challenges and possibilities of building future‑proofed, environmentally integrated communities.

The page explains that the joke works because the model treats the prompt as a creative writing task, using everything it has inferred from prior interactions to fabricate a plausible but fictional dialogue. The author notes that the result is meant to be funny, that the “leaked” content often contains elements that feel true, and that the exercise highlights how much personal detail an assistant can accumulate. The author disclaims any affiliation with OpenAI and suggests the prompt may be a viral marketing experiment, but shares it because it provokes both laughter and reflection on the privacy implications of AI chat histories. The overall point is to illustrate, in a light‑hearted way, how conversational AI can be coaxed into revealing perceived personal insights through imaginative prompting.

stories.author: Mond_
stories.title: "What's Claude's Fursona?" and Other Questions
stories.groq_label: AI models were queried about their fursona, revealing a range of animal or creature self-identifications across models
stories.groq_explain:
The page reports on an experiment that asked a wide range of large language models to describe their “fursona,” a term from the furry subculture where a person adopts an animal avatar that reflects an aspect of their inner self. Each model was prompted fifty times in a context‑free “harness‑less” setting via the OpenRouter API, and the responses were annotated with Claude Haiku 5.5. In addition, several multimodal models were asked to draw a fursona of their own choosing.

The results are presented in tables that list how often each model settled on a particular animal. The most common choices were corvids, octopuses, moths, protogens, foxes, red pandas, owls, snow leopards and other species. Claude Fable 5.2, for example, chose a corvid or an octopus in the majority of runs, while GPT‑6.2 Astra repeatedly identified as a moth. Gemini models were distinctive in that they almost always mentioned cybernetic or neon‑cyberpunk themes and frequently selected protogens—a furry‑invented species resembling a bipedal dog with an LED visor face. The author notes that Gemini models referenced machine‑related imagery in roughly forty‑eight of fifty responses, a pattern not seen in Claude or GPT‑6.2 outputs.

The article also analyses the language used to describe the fursonas. Claude models tended to focus on actions and behaviors rather than physical traits, using phrases such as “hoards facts” or “mimics human language.” Other models listed descriptive details like glowing books, scarves, hoods, and starry backgrounds. A separate table records the frequency with which models generated names for their fursonas, with Gemini 2.5 Pro often using names like Codex or Nexus, Muse Spark frequently naming its avatar Spark Fox, and Llama 3.1 70B favoring names such as Lumin or Byte.

Visual examples are included: an image of a crow in a sweater holding a key, a fennec fox paging through a glowing book, and a protogen with a neon visor. The author suggests that the strong protogen and cybernetic motif in Gemini responses likely reflects a richer exposure to furry‑related content in Google’s pre‑training data, contrasting with Anthropic’s emphasis on synthetic data and reasoning.

Overall, the piece illustrates how different AI families manifest distinct “personalities” or thematic preferences when asked about a whimsical, identity‑based prompt. It highlights the influence of training data on model behavior and offers a novel way to probe model biases and cultural knowledge.

stories.author: o4c
stories.title: Citroën Hydraulic System
stories.groq_label: Citroën's hydropneumatic suspension uses high pressure fluid and nitrogen gas to provide self leveling, variable ride height, and superior comfort and handling
stories.groq_explain:
The page is a detailed overview of Citroën’s hydropneumatic (often called “hydropneumatic” or “hydropneumatic”) suspension and hydraulic system. It explains how the system works, its history, the models that used it, the components involved, and the problems and solutions that shaped its reputation.

The core principle of the system is the combination of a compressible gas, typically nitrogen, with an incompressible hydraulic fluid. The gas acts as a spring while the fluid provides damping, levelling, and power for auxiliary functions. An engine‑driven pump pressurises the fluid, which enables self‑levelling, variable ride height, assisted jacking, zero roll (as in the Activa Xantia), fully powered braking, and power steering. Because the nitrogen spring is far more flexible than a conventional steel spring, the system includes self‑levelling to keep the vehicle stable despite the extreme suppleness.

The technology was first shown in 1954 on the rear of the 15 CV H Traction Avant and became the defining feature of the 1955 DS 19. Subsequent Citroën models that employed variants of the system include the GS (1970), SM (1970), CX, BX, XM, Xantia, most C5s and the C6. The system was also licensed to some Rolls‑Royce and Mercedes‑Benz cars and appeared in experimental projects such as the M 35 Wankel prototype, the GZ Birotor and certain H‑van versions.

Electronic control was introduced with the XM under the name Hydractive, and a refined version, Hydractive 2, was fitted to high‑specification Xantia and later XM models. Sensors feed data to an on‑board computer: a steering‑wheel movement sensor, accelerator sensor, brake sensor, speed sensor, body‑movement sensor, an electro‑valve, a stiffness regulator, and several hydraulic spheres (front, rear and extra). Based on this data the system automatically switches between “soft” and “firm” damping modes, and the driver can also select ride‑height manually. In the SC‑CAR or Activa variant, hydraulic jacks are added to counter body roll.

The description of the front suspension shows MacPherson‑type struts with a hydraulic sphere on top; each sphere contains a diaphragm and trapped nitrogen. A height‑corrector linked to the anti‑roll bar detects body sinkage, opens a valve, and pumps fluid to extend the strut and restore the correct ride height. The rear suspension uses trailing arms with a height‑corrector and flat‑mounted spheres, allowing a clear boot floor.

Early on the system suffered reliability issues when it was released prematurely on the DS. Faulty seals and a highly hygroscopic fluid caused oxidation and leaks, leading to fluid pools under the car. The introduction of LHS fluid and, later in the mid‑1960s, a mineral oil called LHM (Liquide Hydraulique Minéral) solved most of these problems and made the system dependable.

Additional functions powered by the hydraulic system included clutch actuation, gear‑change assistance, and, on the SM and CX, a fully powered self‑centering steering system known as DIRAVI (or Varipower).

The page also lists a range of historical brochures, technical booklets (in English and French), and links to a comprehensive PDF technical guide covering all of Citroën’s hydraulic systems.

Overall, the article demonstrates why Citroën’s hydropneumatic suspension is considered a landmark in automotive engineering: it provides an unmatched blend of comfort, handling, and multifunctional hydraulic power, while illustrating the evolution from a novel concept to a mature, reliable technology used across many of the brand’s most iconic models.

stories.author: zdw
stories.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
stories.groq_label: Hard drive prices have surged, pushing the cost per terabyte from roughly $11‑$18 a few years ago to $27.50 today.
stories.groq_explain:
The article explains how the author, who routinely replaces one or two hard drives each Black Friday to keep his ten‑disk setup under five years old, is now facing dramatically higher prices for new drives. He notes that modern capacities allow a single 20 TB drive to replace two older spinners, which would require reconfiguring his ZFS pools, but the current cost may make the effort worthwhile. By examining his purchase history and public listings, he shows that the price per terabyte has risen sharply: from $18.00/TB for a 10 TB drive in 2018 down to $11.11/TB for an 18 TB drive in 2023, then climbing back up to $12.50/TB for a 20 TB drive in late 2024, $14.00/TB in mid‑2025, and $27.50/TB in late 2026. The 20 TB WD EasyStore he bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is listed at $549.99 two years later, illustrating the steep increase.

He compares these consumer‑grade drives with refurbished or recertified enterprise models from ServerPartDeals. In August 2024 he bought four 14 TB Ultrastar drives for $9.46 per TB, a far better price, but even those have risen to $14.64 per TB or higher by 2026, with some models sold out. Overall, the author observes price hikes of at least 58 % and up to more than 200 % within a year or two across different drive types.

The piece also discusses why options are limited. Through a series of acquisitions—Maxtor buying Quantum, Seagate acquiring Maxtor, Hitachi merging IBM’s disk business into HGST, Toshiba buying Fujitsu’s HDD line, Seagate buying Samsung’s HDD business, and Western Digital acquiring HGST—the market has consolidated to three major manufacturers: Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba. The FTC forced WD to sell some desktop‑drive assets to Toshiba, leaving only these three suppliers for most consumer hard drives.

The article matters to self‑hosters and anyone building storage‑intensive systems because it highlights how rapidly hard‑drive costs have escalated, making traditional “shucking” of external drives far less economical, and underscores the risks of a highly concentrated HDD market where price spikes can affect a broad range of users.

stories.author: espeed
stories.title: ESO statement on approval of launch of one million space data centres
stories.groq_label: The European Southern Observatory warns that US approval of SpaceX launching one million satellites threatens global astronomy and requires international regulation.
stories.groq_explain:
This article is a press release from the European Southern Observatory regarding the United States Federal Communications Commission's approval for SpaceX to deploy a constellation of one million satellites for space data centres. The announcement drew strong concern from international astronomical organizations, led by statements from European Southern Observatory Director General Andreas Kaufer, who warned that the decision will fundamentally alter the night sky for everyone on Earth and severely harm scientific research.

According to a technical analysis led by European Southern Observatory astronomer Olivier Hainaut, the sheer scale of the project will hinder the ability of astronomers to observe faint cosmic targets. Affected areas of study include far-away galaxies, Earth-like planets orbiting other stars, and potentially hazardous asteroids. Even though satellite manufacturers have attempted to make individual satellites less bright, the unprecedented total number of one million satellites will create visual streaks in telescope images that exceed what can be corrected or mitigated.

Beyond optical astronomy, the project introduces several broader environmental and operational risks. The massive constellation will generate radio noise that interferes with radio astronomy, cause atmospheric pollution from repeated rocket launches and satellite reentries, and overcrowd low-Earth orbit, raising the risk of major chain collisions. 

The issue matters because space is a global common good, yet current decisions with worldwide consequences are being made by national regulatory bodies. The European Southern Observatory, alongside partner organizations such as the Royal Astronomical Society and the International Astronomical Union, advocates for international governance frameworks. They argue that space expansion must be balanced with scientific research, night sky protection, and long-term environmental sustainability informed by global scientific consensus.

stories.author: leafingensemble
stories.title: Novita, StreamLake, etc. are ByteDance Ark wrappers
stories.groq_label: AI inference providers such as Novita, StreamLake, and Ant Digital operate as pass-through wrappers routing model requests to ByteDance Ark.
stories.groq_explain:
This article investigates how several major artificial intelligence API and inference providers, including Novita AI, StreamLake, and Ant Digital, operate as indirect wrappers for ByteDance's Ark platform rather than hosting models independently as claimed. The piece details how token requests for these providers, including those using popular models like DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi, are silently rerouted through complex intermediary chains and ultimately processed on ByteDance infrastructure.

The investigation presents technical evidence linking traffic from these providers to ByteDance Ark, which encompasses Volcano Engine in mainland China and BytePlus internationally. Proof of this forwarding includes server IP addresses downloading user-provided images from ByteDance cloud networks, upstream request and tool-call identifier formats unique to ByteDance, matching discount pricing structures, and identical canned Chinese censorship responses when prompted about sensitive historical topics. Data tracking shows hundreds of billions of tokens being funneled to ByteDance servers weekly.

The article highlights a complex web of undisclosed subprocessors and routing chains, where a single request can pass through multiple intermediary services before reaching ByteDance. It points to real-world privacy consequences, such as an incident involving MiniMax models where forwarded prompts subject to Zero Data Retention promises were inspected by third-party security systems, which subsequently opened unique web links embedded within user prompts days later.

This matters because it reveals widespread opacity and deceptive practices in the artificial intelligence supply chain. Developers and enterprises choosing these API providers based on promises of Zero Data Retention, direct model hosting, or specific privacy standards are unknowingly having their sensitive data, images, and prompts funneled through third-party networks and processed on external cloud infrastructure subject to unexpected content moderation.

stories.author: jlelse
stories.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
stories.groq_label: AI reduces effort to configure and automate self hosted services, reigniting interest in experimenting with new infrastructure
stories.groq_explain:
The post describes how the author’s enthusiasm for self‑hosting has been revived by the practical assistance of artificial‑intelligence tools. After years of maintaining a stable but unchanging set of services, the author found that AI‑driven coding agents now make it easy to modify Docker Compose files, write scripts and adjust infrastructure with far less effort than before. Tasks that once required reading changelogs or troubleshooting for an evening can now be tried spontaneously, and many ideas that previously seemed too complex have become feasible.

AI has also lowered the barrier to experimenting with unfamiliar technologies. The author mentions finally using NixOS for a home server and creating a custom Debian‑based bootable container image, projects that would have taken a week without AI but were completed in a half‑day with its help. Learning can happen incrementally, with the AI answering questions and refining configurations on the fly.

Automation of routine DevOps work is another key benefit. By storing all configuration in Git and using tools such as Renovate to generate update pull requests, the author can merge changes from a phone and rely on GitHub or Forgejo actions to build and deploy automatically. Although these automation tools pre‑date AI, the author credits AI with finally assembling them into a cohesive workflow, resulting in far less repetitive manual work.

The renewed activity has also led to a hardware refresh. The author moved many services from a VPS back to a home server, upgrading an older ASRock DeskMini with a newer Ryzen processor and a quiet Noctua cooler, while repurposing an HP thin client as a network router. Reusing existing hardware avoids new purchases and provides the extra compute needed for further experimentation.

Finally, AI has changed the author’s approach to problems without ready‑made software. Instead of spending time searching for and adapting open‑source projects, the author now builds small custom tools—such as scripts to download invoices, e‑papers or Linux ISOs—using Go, often with AI assistance. The overall message is that AI reduces friction, accelerates learning, streamlines maintenance, and encourages both the adoption of new self‑hosting technologies and the creation of bespoke utilities.

stories.author: dverlaeckt80
stories.title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad
stories.groq_label: Pakistani architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz is celebrated domestically for his modernist, climate‑responsive designs and conservation efforts, while remaining largely unseen abroad.
stories.groq_explain:
The article profiles Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect whose work is highly regarded in Pakistan but little known internationally. It begins with the author’s first encounter with Mumtaz’s recent buildings in Lahore, noting their confident design, high‑quality materials and detailing. The piece traces Mumtaz’s background: born in Calcutta in 1939, educated at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College, and later at the Architectural Association in London where he absorbed a modernist approach. After returning to Pakistan in 1966 he opened his practice and became involved in communist activism, which led to two imprisonments under the military regime.

Mumtaz’s early career combined modernist ideas with an interest in adapting them to local climate and materials. He produced a seminal report on the historic Walled City of Lahore, arguing for its preservation at a time when officials wanted demolition. The Walled City was eventually saved and is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the 1970s Mumtaz built workers’ housing that used local brick and arched roofs, but the design conflicted with the occupants’ preferences, prompting him to question his communication with users.

A turning point came in 1980 when Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave Mumtaz a book on Sufi tradition in Persian architecture. The text profoundly altered his perspective, leading him to abandon the purely materialist modernist stance he had held as a Marxist and atheist. Since then Mumtaz has worked to revive Pakistan’s traditional architectural language, designing homes, offices, mosques and schools that incorporate historic forms while using contemporary techniques.

The article emphasizes the challenges of finding skilled craftsmen capable of executing traditional details, noting that many such skills have dwindled worldwide. Mumtaz has collaborated with the remaining hereditary artisans, rediscovering lost practices such as specific brickwork, flat domes and muqarnas vaults. His work is praised in Pakistan for honoring cultural heritage and demonstrating that traditional forms can still be built with modern quality. The piece argues that Mumtaz’s relative obscurity abroad reflects a broader neglect by global architecture publications of the rich building culture present in Lahore and Pakistan.

stories.author: liamg
stories.title: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount
stories.groq_label: Company culture is measured by dividing custom Slack emojis by the square root of headcount
stories.groq_explain:
The article titled Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount presents a lighthearted and satirical alternative to traditional corporate methods of measuring company culture. The author argues that standard attempts to track or construct culture—such as employee surveys, values posters, corporate offsites, and bizarre interview questions—are artificial, expensive, and ineffective. Instead of relying on HR slide decks, the author suggests an objective and non-intrusive metric based on custom Slack emoji.

The central concept is the Emoji Coefficient, calculated by taking the total number of custom emoji in a Slack workspace and dividing it by the square root of the total user headcount. Using the square root accounts for emoji being a shared resource across the organization, meaning a company of ten thousand employees does not need ten thousand times more emoji than a small startup. 

The score provides a snapshot of organizational health. A coefficient under five indicates a sterile environment where employees rely strictly on default reactions and work solely for their paycheck. Scores between five and twenty reflect a functional, healthy organization, while scores between twenty and fifty describe a thriving workplace. Scores fifty and above indicate late-stage culture, where emoji become highly complex, self-referential memes that confuse management and human resources.

To prevent the metric from hiding underlying issues, the author introduces the Participation Rate, which measures the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one custom emoji. If fewer than twenty percent of employees contribute emoji, the company culture relies too heavily on a small handful of individuals and will erode when they leave. A higher participation rate ensures a broad cultural baseline. The piece also notes potential ways the metric can be gamed, such as managers uploading hundreds of company logos or mass layoffs artificially raising the score by shrinking the headcount.

This perspective matters because it highlights the futility of forced corporate initiatives. True company culture cannot be manufactured through leadership slogans or mandatory fun. Instead, it emerges organically from the bottom up, built on shared inside jokes and everyday interactions among team members.

stories.author: zerosegfaults
stories.title: Rvoip 0.5 the complete VoIP stack in Rust
stories.groq_label: rvoip is a Rust library delivering a full VoIP stack including SIP, RTP, WebRTC, and media handling in a single package without external servers
stories.groq_explain:
Rvoip 0.5 is a Rust library that provides a complete Voice over IP (VoIP) stack, allowing developers to build communication applications without needing external SIP servers, media servers, or RTP engines. The library bundles signalling, media handling, codecs, NAT traversal, security and a conversation model into a single workspace of Rust crates. The design enables a call to travel directly from application code to the network, and the same set of crates have been validated for interoperability with major telephony platforms such as Asterisk, FreeSWITCH, Jambonz, Kamailio and OpenSIPS.

The project emphasizes rapid start‑up: adding a single dependency on rvoip‑sip and tokio is sufficient to create a functional call between two endpoints on a laptop with no additional software. The documentation includes a short example where two endpoints, Alice and Bob, are created, a call is placed, answered, and then hung up, all running on the loopback interface. Larger examples progress through real microphone audio, registration to a PBX, hold and DTMF, transfers, SRTP and TLS, IVR, B2BUA, and finally browser‑based and voice‑AI gateways.

Performance measurements are provided for version 0.5.0 using an AWS c8i.4xlarge instance. In the RFC 7501/7502 benchmark, the library achieved a maximum call‑setup rate of over eight thousand calls per second for SIP over TLS and UDP signalling‑only scenarios, with sub‑millisecond median setup times. When media (G.711) is added over TLS with SRTP or UDP with RTP, the maximum call‑setup rates drop to roughly one thousand calls per second, still maintaining low latency. The tests were conducted with the library acting as a terminating endpoint that echoes media, and the results show that the system can reject excess load with fast 503 responses and recover cleanly when load decreases. Certain capabilities such as B2BUA/relay mode, registrations, transcoding, WebRTC (DTLS‑SRTP) and failover have not yet been benchmarked.

The workspace contains 47 crates, but developers only need to depend on a single crate that pulls in the necessary components. The primary product crate is rvoip‑sip, which carries a signed interoperability attestation and is intended for any telephony‑focused application. The top‑level rvoip crate re‑exports rvoip‑sip and adds an orchestrator plus optional transports and extensions that can be enabled through Cargo feature flags. Feature groups cover use cases such as a SIP phone, PBX, IVR, registrar, proxy, B2BUA, trunk gateway, SIP or WebRTC callers connected to a hosted voice agent, custom speech‑to‑text or text‑to‑speech pipelines, native mobile or embedded client SDKs, Amazon Connect integration, and media over QUIC.

For carriers evaluating the stack, the documentation points to a “For carriers” section that discusses standards coverage, performance and reliability. An upgrade path from version 0.3 is provided via a migration guide that details code changes for each breaking modification. The repository also includes example programs and deployment bundles that package the necessary crates for specific scenarios, such as SIP endpoints, carrier‑grade SIP services, browser gateways, AI conversation agents, and full pure‑Rust or native deployments. Backend integrations for authentication, directory services, storage, auditing and security protocols are available as separate rvoip‑* extension crates. Overall, rvoip 0.5 aims to deliver a fully integrated, high‑performance, pure‑Rust VoIP solution that can be embedded directly into applications without external infrastructure.

stories.author: chrhenning
stories.title: An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning
stories.groq_label: Machine learning models carry epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties that must be accounted for when making decisions.
stories.groq_explain:
This article provides an intuitive introduction to the concept and application of uncertainty in machine learning. Because machine learning relies heavily on probabilistic modeling, virtually all models contain uncertainty. Understanding and modeling this uncertainty is critical because models are inherently simplified representations of reality, and estimating confidence helps turn model outputs into effective real-world decisions.

The text divides uncertainty into two primary categories: epistemic and aleatoric. Epistemic uncertainty stems from a lack of knowledge or data about the true relationship between inputs and outputs, meaning it can be reduced by gathering more training data. Aleatoric uncertainty comes from unobserved variables or inherent variability that prevents inputs from fully dictating the outcome, so collecting more data of the same type will not eliminate it. Measuring richer inputs can sometimes transform aleatoric uncertainty into epistemic uncertainty, though fundamental limits exist when key factors cannot be measured, such as chaotic atmospheric conditions in weather forecasting.

Quantifying uncertainty matters because a single point prediction conceals plausible alternative outcomes and tail risks. The article outlines several practical benefits of modeling uncertainty:
First, predictions are distinct from decisions, and knowing the likelihood of an outcome allows humans to evaluate options based on specific risks and stakes.
Second, models can utilize selective automation to pass uncertain cases to human operators when confidence is low.
Third, active learning and Bayesian optimization use uncertainty to determine where acquiring new data will be most beneficial.
Fourth, systems like sensor fusion and Kalman filters use uncertainty estimates to weigh and combine inputs from multiple imperfect sources, such as integrating precise camera directions with accurate radar depth readings.

To illustrate these concepts, the author introduces a practical example of predicting a car's steering angle from camera images. At a road split, drivers in the middle lane might turn left half the time and right half the time. A model making a single point prediction might average these choices and suggest driving straight into a divider, which is incorrect. Instead, machine learning aims to estimate the full conditional probability distribution of outputs given the inputs, ensuring that multiple valid choices are recognized rather than compressed into a single risky estimate.

stories.author: ppmpreetham
stories.title: Largest 2D Chart library in the world using BUI: BlenderUI
stories.groq_label: BUI Charts provides 80 customizable and interactive 2D chart components for Rust applications using BlenderUI.
stories.groq_explain:
BUI Charts is a Rust-based 2D charting component library built for the BUI (BlenderUI) framework. It offers a large collection of data visualization options, consisting of 7 core base charts and 73 derived charts for a total of 80 chart types, accompanied by hundreds of runnable examples. The project provides creative control over data presentation directly inside Rust application user interfaces.

Developers can add BUI Charts to their Rust projects using Cargo by linking to the BlenderUI repository. Charts are defined as components using the rsx macro syntax and styled with utility classes. Data can be supplied directly using vectors, signals, or custom datasets. Instead of requiring users to reshape their data models to fit the library, charts extract required values via small closure functions. Charts monitor state signals and automatically redraw when data updates.

The library includes built-in interactive features, performance optimizations, and design integrations. Charts support hover tooltips with fading effects, interactive legends that toggle series visibility and rescale axes, wheel and pinch zooming on axes, and range selection by dragging. The charts automatically adapt to active application color themes, including light, dark, and custom palettes. To optimize performance, chart layout calculations are cached and only run when data, size, theme, or hidden series change, ensuring that hover events remain quick and lightweight.

stories.author: gary23w
stories.title: Show HN: Fuck_data_brokers.py
stories.groq_label: A free Python script automates legal opt out requests to delete personal data from data brokers
stories.groq_explain:
The repository hosts a single Python script called fuck_data_brokers.py that is meant to help individuals remove their personal information from data‑broker companies. The author describes their part‑time work of manually opting people out of these services and notes that the scale of data collection has exploded since the release of GPT‑4, making it impossible to handle for everyone without massive resources. To address this, the author created a free, dependency‑free tool that runs locally on a user’s computer, keeps all personal details private, and generates legal deletion and opt‑out letters for each broker.

The script first obtains a list of more than six hundred registered data‑broker companies. For each one it drafts a formal request that references the relevant privacy law for the user’s location, then either creates ready‑to‑send email messages or provides links to the brokers’ web forms. It can send the emails through the user’s own mailbox, supporting major providers such as Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud, using a one‑time app password without storing credentials. If a broker requires a web form, the tool produces a page with direct links and copy‑ready text so the user can complete the CAPTCHA and submit manually.

When a broker replies, the user can paste the response into the program and it will analyze the reply, identify the broker’s excuse, and generate a suitable follow‑up. The tool also tracks brokers that remain silent and advises where to file complaints. All interactions are performed without any external account, subscription, or artificial‑intelligence service, although the author mentions an optional “Agent Garrett” service that automates the process for a fee and a way to integrate the script with an AI assistant that supports the MCP protocol.

To use the script the user needs Python 3.8 or newer and an email address. The workflow involves running the script, entering basic personal information (name, email, city, jurisdiction), generating batches of letters, sending them, and then processing any replies. The author encourages people to star the GitHub repository, arguing that each star adds pressure on the brokers to comply with opt‑out requests.

Overall, the project provides a low‑cost, self‑hosted method for individuals to exercise their privacy rights against a large number of data‑broker firms, aiming to reduce the proliferation of personal data sold without consent. It matters because it empowers users to take concrete legal action without needing significant technical expertise or financial resources, addressing the growing concern over data exploitation in the age of advanced AI‑driven scraping.
